questions.q: What was the natural magnet known to ancients?
questions.a: Magnetite, a stone that attracts iron - legend of a shepherd Magnes whose stick stuck to a rock.

questions.q: Where was magnetite discovered?
questions.a: In a region called Magnesia (in ancient Greece/Turkey); also in India long ago.

questions.q: What is a natural magnet?
questions.a: A naturally occurring magnetic stone - magnetite, an iron ore.

questions.q: What are magnetic materials? Give examples.
questions.a: Materials attracted by magnets - iron, nickel, cobalt (and steel).

questions.q: Name three non-magnetic materials.
questions.a: Wood, plastic, glass (also paper, copper).

questions.q: How can you find whether a material is magnetic?
questions.a: Bring a magnet near - attraction shows the material is magnetic.

questions.q: What are the poles of a magnet?
questions.a: The two ends where magnetic strength is greatest - north and south poles.

questions.q: Where is a magnet's pull strongest?
questions.a: At its poles - iron filings cluster there.

questions.q: What happens when a magnet is hung freely?
questions.a: It settles with one pole (north-seeking) toward the earth's north.

concepts.title: Directive Property of a Freely Suspended Magnet

questions.q: What happens when a bar magnet is suspended freely?
questions.a: It always comes to rest roughly in the north-south direction.

questions.q: Which end of a freely hanging magnet points north?
questions.a: The north-seeking pole (north pole) of the magnet.

questions.q: How did this property of magnets help sailors?
questions.a: It gave the compass - sailors found direction at sea.

questions.q: What is a magnetic compass?
questions.a: A small magnetic needle pivoted freely in a case, used to find directions.

questions.q: How does a compass show direction?
questions.a: Its needle settles north-south; the marked north end points to the north.

questions.q: What makes the compass needle turn?
questions.a: Any nearby magnet or magnetic material deflects the needle.

questions.q: How is an artificial magnet made by single-touch method?
questions.a: Rubbing a steel bar repeatedly with one pole of a magnet in one direction makes the bar a magnet.

questions.q: Name two other ways of making magnets.
questions.a: Double-touch rubbing and electrical method (current through a coil around iron).

questions.q: Why do artificial magnets lose power over time?
questions.a: Heat, hammering and rough handling disturb their magnetism - proper storage keeps them strong.

questions.q: What happens when like poles of two magnets meet?
questions.a: They repel each other - push apart.

questions.q: What happens when unlike poles come near?
questions.a: They attract - pull together.

questions.q: How can you identify two identical-looking iron bars, one magnetised?
questions.a: Bring one's end to the other's middle: the magnet attracts the middle of plain iron; if it repels anywhere, both ends show poles.

questions.q: How should magnets be stored?
questions.a: In pairs with opposite poles together, with soft iron keepers across the ends, away from heat.

questions.q: Name two things that weaken a magnet.
questions.a: Heating and hammering (also rough storage near other magnets).

questions.q: Why should magnets be kept away from mobiles and computers?
questions.a: Their magnetism can disturb electronic devices and screens.
